strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across multiple video understanding benchmarks (6 benchmarks, 3 domains) with detailed ablation studies
Extensive scaling analysis and insights into learned attention patterns, including gating distributions and attention sink behavior
Solid engineering contribution with clear hybrid approach combining sparse attention for vision and dense attention for text
Demonstrates effective scaling beyond training length (36K trained → 128K inference)
Thorough ablations convincingly show all three branches are necessary
Good reproducibility effort with detailed training hyperparameters and evaluation settings
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing NSA (Yuan et al., 2025b) to video domain without algorithmic innovations
Modest empirical improvements over existing sparse baselines (often <2 points: LVB +0.9, MLVU +1.6, TimeScope +0.6)
Claimed improvements on spatial understanding contradicted by results (VSIBench: -0.5 points vs XAttention), undermining credibility

Confounded experimental setup: uses filtered 216K training subset while baseline also trained on same data but underperforms, making it unclear if improvements come from architecture or training details
Incomplete efficiency analysis: reports 3.6% attention budget but provides no end-to-end inference time/throughput comparisons, only individual branch latency (Figure 6)
Dense-NSA baseline (Table 3) shows sparse-trained weights benefit dense attention, suggesting learned representations may be primary benefit rather than sparsity mechanism itself

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across multiple benchmarks and three distinct domains (long-form video, temporal reasoning, spatial understanding)
Extensive empirical analysis with detailed ablations, layer-wise visualizations, and task-specific performance investigations
Practical efficiency achievement of 3.6% attention budget utilization with reasonable performance
Thorough supplementary material with detailed subtask-level results and additional experiments
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: directly applies existing NSA method (Yuan et al., 2025b) to video with straightforward hybrid attention, offering no fundamental methodological innovations
Marginal and inconsistent improvements across benchmarks (1-3% on most benchmarks, sometimes underperforming existing sparse attention baselines like MInference and XAttention)

Baseline comparison concerns: fine-tuned Dense-SFT baseline (57.8) performs worse than original baseline (58.7), suggesting suboptimal tuning; unclear if other sparse methods received equivalent training protocols
High model sensitivity to attention allocation (Finding 3) is presented as insight but represents a significant limitation requiring per-task hyperparameter tuning with no principled selection method
Efficiency claims overstated: claims 'near-linear scalability' but Figure 6 shows compression branch dominates latency without linear scaling; no end-to-end latency/throughput comparisons provided
Insufficient justification for hybrid design: no ablation demonstrating that dense text attention is necessary; claim that sparse attention hurts instruction following is unsupported

Unfair evaluation setup: model trained with specific constraints (4 fps, 350-550 frames, 36K tokens) but evaluated with benchmark-specific different configurations (Table 5); reproducibility of filtered 216K dataset uncertain

Analysis lacks depth: findings are largely descriptive rather than explanatory; attention sink analysis doesn't clearly establish why dynamic gating helps beyond empirical observation; no statistical significance testing despite small margin improvements
Computational cost not addressed: 4600 H100 GPU hours training investment for marginal improvements; no comparison of total cost (training + inference) vs. performance gains versus alternatives
Missing critical comparisons: Video-XL-2 outperforms VideoNSA on LongVideoBench (61.0 vs 60.0) with limited discussion; recent 2025 methods not thoroughly engaged

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across 6 benchmarks and 3 domains with systematic comparison to token compression and sparse attention baselines
Thorough experimental analysis including branch ablations, information/attention budget scaling, gate weight analysis, and attention sink investigation
Well-motivated hybrid attention design preserving dense attention for text while applying learnable sparse attention to video tokens
Strong reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, evaluation settings, and extensive appendices; achieves 3.6% attention budget efficiency
Technically sound approach combining three complementary sparse branches with data-dependent learnable gating; demonstrates reliable extrapolation beyond training length
Six detailed empirical findings provide valuable insights beyond performance reporting, particularly regarding task-dependent allocation and attention sink mitigation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primary contribution is adapting existing NSA (Yuan et al., 2025b) to video; hybrid attention and frame-based blocking are engineering rather than conceptual innovations

Modest empirical improvements over baselines—typically 0.5-0.6 points (LongVideoBench: 60.0 vs 59.5, MLVU: 51.8 vs 51.2); actually underperforms on VSIBench (36.1 vs 36.6). Gains are consistent but incremental

Insufficient computational analysis: no wall-clock inference time comparison, FLOPs, or memory consumption analysis despite 4600 H100-hour training cost. Compression branch identified as bottleneck but not compared quantitatively to baselines

Significant sensitivity to configuration shown in Findings 2-3: optimal global-local attention allocation is highly task-dependent and model remains sensitive to attention scaling, limiting practical generalizability

All experiments use single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B); generalization to different vision encoders or LLMs unexplored. Table 3 shows sparse-trained weights provide limited benefit when transferred to dense attention

Incomplete comparison with concurrent work: Video-XL-2 (Qin et al., 2025b) mentioned only briefly; no comparison with Mamba-based approaches despite being highly relevant to efficient video understanding

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 diverse benchmarks spanning long-form video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding with systematic comparison to strong baselines
Thorough ablation studies and analysis including branch combinations, context/attention scaling, layer-wise gating patterns, and attention sink characterization that provide actionable insights
Strong performance on specific challenging tasks (Tomato: 26.5 vs 23.0 for best baseline; ultra-long video understanding with 10-hour videos) demonstrating practical value
Highly reproducible with detailed hyperparameters, training settings, evaluation configurations, and comprehensive supplementary material (40+ pages)
Well-motivated modality-specific design (sparse attention for vision, dense for text) that balances efficiency with instruction-following capability
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily applies existing Native Sparse Attention (Yuan et al., 2025c) to video domain. The three branches (compression, selection, sliding window) and dynamic gating are from prior work. Main contribution reduces to modality-specific attention split, which is incremental

Modest performance improvements on most benchmarks (LongVideoBench +0.9%, MLVU +1.6%, TimeScope +0.6%), within typical LLM evaluation variance. Raises question about whether added complexity is justified

Concerning baseline setup: Dense-SFT fine-tuned baseline shows performance drops compared to base Qwen2.5-VL on multiple benchmarks (Table 3), suggesting potential fine-tuning issues and undermining fairness of comparisons

High sensitivity and limited generalizability: Method is extremely sensitive to attention allocation (1-2% swings in Figure 3), optimal configuration is task-dependent, and results are strongest near training configuration, requiring per-task tuning

Significant theory-practice efficiency gap: Ideal 0.24× FLOPs speedup vs actual 0.56× achieved, with Qwen architecture padding overhead and compression branch bottleneck limiting practical speedup claims

Limited architectural scope: Evaluation only on Qwen2.5-VL-7B with no evaluation on other VLM architectures (LLaVA, InternVL) or models with different head configurations, raising generalization concerns

Training data concerns: Filtered to only 216K from 961K pairs (22.5%) with arbitrary thresholds (350-550 frames, 4 fps). No justification for filtering criteria; evaluation on unfiltered data would strengthen claims
Statistical significance not reported: No error bars, confidence intervals, significance testing, or explicit mention of multiple runs, making it unclear if small improvements are reliable

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across three task domains (long video understanding, temporal reasoning, spatial understanding) with multiple benchmarks
Extensive ablation studies and analysis including branch selection, information scaling, attention budget allocation, and gate weight visualization
Demonstrates scalability to 128K tokens with only 3.6% of full attention budget
Well-motivated problem identifying context length limitations in video-language models
Detailed analysis of attention sinks across different branches with clear visualization
weaknesses: Limited novelty: straightforward application of existing NSA (Yuan et al., 2025c) to video with standard training procedure; core sparse attention mechanisms are unchanged from prior work

Modest and inconsistent empirical improvements: competitive but not clearly superior to simpler baselines (e.g., 60.0 vs. 59.5 on LongVideoBench, 83.7 vs. 83.1 on TimeScope); no statistical significance testing

Overstated efficiency claims: substantial gap between theoretical FLOPs (0.24× of Flash Attention) and actual implementation (0.56×, a 2.3× gap); latency advantage only appears at 64K+ tokens, not throughout
Unjustified computational overhead: 4600 H100 GPU hours training cost not adequately justified by modest performance margins; paper acknowledges 0.87× of dense baseline but this is still prohibitive

Analysis lacks actionable insights: Section 4 presents six 'findings' that are primarily post-hoc observations (e.g., Finding 3 essentially states optimal allocation is near training config, which is tautological) rather than novel scientific insights
Reproducibility issues: Code, model, and project page links are blank; missing details on convergence, training stability, and hyperparameter sensitivity
Missing statistical validation: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; results appear to be single runs
Limited generalization analysis: evaluation on only one backbone (Qwen2.5-VL); unclear if approach transfers to other video-language models

Presentation clarity: paper is extremely dense with six major findings and extensive appendix, making core contribution difficult to extract; some overclaiming (e.g., 'near-linear scalability' not well-supported by actual latency results)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (LongVideoBench, MLVU, TimeScope, LongTimeScope, Tomato, VSIBench) with rigorous ablation studies
Thorough analysis providing six distinct findings with detailed visualizations of attention patterns, gate distributions, and attention sink behaviors
Technically sound approach with appropriate modality-aware design (sparse for vision, dense for text) and principled adaptation of NSA to video
Practical efficiency gains with near-linear scaling to 128K tokens using only 3.6% of attention budget
Strong reproducibility effort with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, and 40+ page appendix
Interesting technical insights about dynamic gating's role in mitigating attention sinks and modality-specific sparsity patterns
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primary contribution is adapting existing NSA method to video; hybrid attention design is intuitive but not conceptually novel
Modest performance improvements on most benchmarks (0.5-2% gains on LVB, MLVU, TimeScope; larger gains only on Tomato at 15.2%)
Unfair baseline comparisons: VideoNSA is end-to-end trained while most baselines are training-free; Dense-SFT baseline underperforms original, raising questions about training setup

Practical efficiency gains are overstated: theoretical FLOPs (0.24×) differ significantly from actual FLOPs (0.56×); wall-clock speedups (3.1-4.1×) are competitive but not exceptional with other sparse methods
High sensitivity to attention budget configuration with significant performance drops outside training settings; optimal allocation is task-dependent without clear a priori guidance
Extrapolation limited: performance sometimes peaks at 64K and decreases at 128K, contradicting scalability claims; model requires careful tuning for new domains
Post-hoc and informal theoretical justification (Appendix M on routing-path stability and RoPE); design choices appear empirically driven without principled rationale
Training on filtered dataset (216K from 961K with specific constraints) may introduce bias; generalization to unconstrained videos unclear
